topics: 🍇 Orlah and Kilayim Combine — but Rabbi Shimon holds no measure is needed for lashes at all
🧵 Garment, Sack, Hide, and Mat — combining by Rabbi Shimon's 'fit for a zav's seat' logic
💍 New Chapter, New Mishna — Rabbi Akiva vs. the Rabbis: does me'ilah require actual damage?

📜 One Verse, Many Rules — deriving the anatomy of me'ilah through a gezeirah shava with teruma

overview.title: 📖 Overview: A New Chapter on the Nature of Misuse
overview.subtitle: Meilah 18a–18b
overview.hebrewSource: הַנֶּהֱנֶה מִן הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם – מָעַל, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the fourth chapter's discussion of combining measures — orlah and kilayim, and garments of different materials — before opening a new chapter with its central mishna: does me'ilah require actually damaging consecrated property, or does mere benefit suffice? Rabbi Akiva says any peruta's worth of benefit is enough; the Rabbis distinguish items that CAN be damaged (requiring peruta-worth of damage) from those that cannot (where benefit alone suffices). Rava narrows down exactly where they truly disagree. The daf then presents an extensive baraita deriving, through a verbal analogy to teruma, the essential structure of me'ilah: who is liable, what 'ma'al' means, and a whole set of technical requirements — and their surprising exceptions.

slides.title: 🍇🧵 Closing the Chapter: Two More Combining Mishnayot
slides.subtitle: Forbidden produce mixtures, and materials that become impure
rows: Orlah (first-three-years fruit) + kilayim (diverse-kinds grain), mixed into permitted produce
They combine to reach the threshold that forbids the mixture (per the mishna's first opinion)
Rabbi Shimon's view on the above
Emended to mean: they need NOT combine — he holds one is flogged for eating even less than the minimum measure, since the olive-bulk measure applies only to the requirement for an offering
Garment (3x3 handbreadths) + sack (4x4) + hide (5x5) + mat (6x6)
All combine with each other to reach the LARGER of the two measures involved
Rabbi Shimon's reason for the above
All these materials are equally fit to become impure through a zav sitting on them (a shared, smaller measure) — that shared fitness is what allows them to combine for other impurities too

slides.title: 💍 New Mishna: Does Me'ilah Require Damage?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Akiva vs. the Rabbis

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Deriving a peruta's worth of benefit from consecrated property is ALWAYS me'ilah — even if nothing was damaged.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: It depends on the item: if it's the KIND of thing that gets damaged by use, one isn't liable until he causes a peruta's worth of damage. If it's the kind that does NOT get damaged by use, benefit alone triggers me'ilah.

lines.speaker: Examples (damage-free)
lines.text: Wearing a consecrated necklace or ring, or drinking from a gold cup — these aren't worn down by use, so ALL agree: benefit alone is enough.

lines.speaker: Examples (damage-prone)
lines.text: Wearing a consecrated robe, covering oneself with a garment, or chopping wood with a consecrated ax — these ARE worn down by use, so no me'ilah until a peruta's worth of actual damage.

callout.label: Parallel rule:
callout.text: A LIVE sin offering (which could still be redeemed, hence 'damaged' in value) needs a peruta of damage; a DEAD one (no redemption possible) triggers me'ilah from any benefit at all.

slides.title: 👕 Rava Locates the Real Disagreement
slides.subtitle: Both sides actually agree more than the mishna first suggests
slides.hebrewSource: מוֹדֶה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא לַחֲכָמִים בְּדָבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ פְּגָם
slides.label: Rava's clarification:
slides.text: A baraita reveals that Rabbi Akiva actually CONCEDES to the Rabbis for items that can be damaged. So what's left to disagree about? Rava explains: for OUTER garments (exposed to weather) and INNER garments (touching skin, worn by sweat), everyone agrees damage is required, since wear is obvious and cumulative. The real dispute is about a MIDDLE garment (neither fully exposed nor against the skin) and fine, expensive fabric (malmala) — items where wear happens so slowly or carefully that no measurable depreciation accrues. There, Rabbi Akiva says benefit alone still triggers me'ilah; the Rabbis insist on actual peruta-level damage regardless.

slides.title: 📜 The Gezeirah Shava: Me'ilah Modeled on Teruma
slides.subtitle: A single shared word — 'sin' (חֵטְא) — unlocks the technical structure of misuse
rows: Damage AND benefit must both occur
One is liable only when both damaging and deriving benefit happen (not damage alone, not benefit alone)
The same person who damaged must be the one who benefited
No liability if one person damages and a different person benefits
Benefit must come from the very item damaged
No 'mixing' benefit from one item with damage to another
Damage and benefit must occur simultaneously
They cannot be separated in time as distinct events
Applies only to something detached from the ground
Land or attached property is excluded from me'ilah under this analogy
An agent who properly performs his mission acts for the sender
The one who APPOINTED the agent, not the agent himself, bears liability for the me'ilah

callout.label: Also derived independently:
callout.text: 'Anyone' (נֶפֶשׁ) in the verse includes the ordinary individual, the king, AND the anointed High Priest equally — all share the same me'ilah liability despite differing in other obligations.

slides.title: 📜 Then the Analogy Breaks — On Purpose
slides.subtitle: 'If anyone commits a misuse' (תִּמְעֹל מַעַל) overrides several of teruma's own limits

steps.content: 1️⃣ Teruma's model would require damage-and-benefit to be the SAME item — but 'תמעל מעל' teaches misuse liability applies even without a damageable item at all
2️⃣ Teruma's model wouldn't combine two SEPARATE acts of consumption — but me'ilah DOES: eating half an olive-bulk today and half tomorrow (even much later) still combines to create liability
3️⃣ Teruma's model requires ONE person's damage to match their OWN benefit — but me'ilah combines: one person's consumption WITH another's, even years apart, still adding up to a peruta
4️⃣ Each expansion is anchored in the same inclusive phrase — 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' teaches liability 'in any case,' overriding what the teruma-analogy alone would have restricted

callout.label: The method:
callout.text: The Gemara builds structure through one verbal analogy, then immediately widens it through the verse's own inclusive language — showing me'ilah is both technically precise and deliberately expansive.

summary.principle: Me'ilah's core structure is borrowed from teruma's 'sin' — requiring matched damage and benefit by the same person from the same item at the same moment — but the Torah's own inclusive phrasing then widens several of those limits, allowing separate acts of consumption, by different people, over long stretches of time, to combine into a single act of liability.

flowSteps.content: 🍇🧵 Orlah/kilayim and multi-material garments combine to their measures, closing the chapter
💍 New mishna: R' Akiva says benefit alone suffices; Rabbis require actual damage for damageable items
👕 Rava: true dispute is narrow — only middle garments and fine fabric, not obvious wear-and-tear items

columns.content: 📜 Gezeirah shava from teruma: same person, same item, simultaneous, detached, agent's sender liable
📜 But 'תמעל מעל' expands: combines across time and across people despite teruma's stricter model

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: me'ilah's technical skeleton comes from one analogy, but its true reach is set by the Torah's own broader language

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is the core dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis regarding me'ilah?
o: Whether me'ilah applies to the King
Whether deriving a peruta's worth of benefit alone (without actual damage) constitutes me'ilah for items that CAN be damaged by use
Whether sin offerings can ever be subject to me'ilah
Whether priests are exempt from me'ilah
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva holds benefit alone always creates liability; the Rabbis distinguish items that can be damaged (requiring actual peruta-level damage) from those that cannot (where benefit alone suffices) — though a baraita reveals Rabbi Akiva actually concedes on damageable items in some cases.

quiz.q: According to Rava, where do Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis actually disagree, given that Rabbi Akiva concedes for ordinary damageable items?
o: They disagree about gold jewelry only
They disagree specifically about middle garments and fine, expensive fabric, where wear is not measurably cumulative
They disagree about sin offerings only
There is no real disagreement between them
quiz.e: Rava narrows the dispute to garments that are neither clearly outer (weather-exposed) nor inner (sweat-worn) — middle garments and fine fabric — where damage doesn't accrue in an obvious, measurable way.

quiz.q: Through the verbal analogy ('sin') between teruma and me'ilah, what is one requirement the baraita derives?
o: That only priests can commit me'ilah
That the same person who caused the damage must be the one who derived the benefit, from the very item damaged, simultaneously
That me'ilah applies only on Shabbat
That me'ilah requires three witnesses
quiz.e: The gezeirah shava teaches several parallel requirements from teruma, including that the damage and benefit must occur to the same person, from the same item, and at the same time.

quiz.q: How does the phrase 'תִּמְעֹל מַעַל' (if anyone commits a misuse) expand beyond what the teruma analogy alone would allow?
o: It has no expansive effect
It allows separate acts of consumption — by the same person over time, or by different people entirely — to combine toward the peruta threshold, even though teruma's model would not allow this
It exempts the king from liability
It limits me'ilah to only detached items, nothing else
quiz.e: The inclusive phrase overrides teruma's stricter same-person, same-time model, allowing combination of consumption across time (even years) and across different people.

quiz.q: What is the difference in me'ilah liability between deriving benefit from a live sin offering versus a dead one?
o: There is no difference
A live sin offering requires a peruta's worth of damage (since it could still be redeemed); a dead one triggers me'ilah from any benefit at all (since it can no longer be redeemed)
A dead sin offering is never subject to me'ilah
A live sin offering is never subject to me'ilah
quiz.e: The mishna parallels this to the damage/no-damage distinction: a live sin offering retains redeemable value that can be 'damaged,' while a dead one cannot be redeemed, so any benefit at all constitutes me'ilah.
